pages.text: VERA original development packet. Linear algebra: a transformation is represented by a 2 by 2 matrix A. The first column is the image of (1,0), and the second is the image of (0,1). Matrix-vector multiplication transforms coordinates. A nonzero vector v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue lambda when Av=lambda v. Compute eigenvalues using det(A-lambda I)=0. For a 2 by 2 matrix the trace is a+d and determinant is ad-bc. Distinct real eigenvalues have independent eigendirections. This sheet supplies course scope only; it is not an instructor assessment or evidence of an upcoming exam's format.

scenario.title: Northstar calibration report
scenario.context: A fictional imaging lab calibrates a linear coordinate transformation. Measurements use dimensionless coordinates. The same transformation applies to every recorded vector. The exhibits contain synthetic practice data.

exam.title: Eigenvalues & transformations
exam.instructions: Answer all questions. Show your working for free responses. Refer to the synthetic transformation-lab exhibits.

questions.question: Using the matrix in the calibration sheet, which value is the determinant of the lab's transformation?
questions.solution: For a two-by-two matrix, $\det(A)=ad-bc=3\cdot3-1\cdot1=8$. Option A is correct.

questions.question: Using the calibration sheet, which value is an eigenvalue of the transformation?
questions.solution: The characteristic equation is $(3-\lambda)^2-1=0$, so $\lambda=4$ or $2$. Option A is correct.

questions.question: A new calibration probe starts at coordinates (2, -1). Use the shared transformation matrix to find its image. Is this probe an eigenvector? Justify your answer using the two coordinate ratios.
questions.solution: $A(2,-1)^T=(5,-1)^T$. The coordinate ratios are $5/2$ and $1$, which are unequal. No single scalar maps the input to that output, so this probe is not an eigenvector.

questions.question: From the calibration matrix, find both eigenvalues and give a corresponding nonzero eigenvector for each. Explain how the diagram reflects the invariant directions.
questions.solution: $\det(A-\lambda I)=(3-\lambda)^2-1=0$, giving $\lambda_1=4$ and $\lambda_2=2$. Direct multiplication gives $A(1,1)^T=(4,4)^T$ and $A(1,-1)^T=(2,-2)^T$. These nonzero vectors keep their directions, scaled by their respective eigenvalues.

questions.question: Use the two basis-probe measurements in the vector table to reconstruct the transformation matrix. Explain why those two measurements determine its action on any vector, then state its trace.
questions.solution: The images of the standard basis vectors are the columns of $A$, so $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$. For any $(x,y)^T$, linearity gives $A(x,y)^T=xA(1,0)^T+yA(0,1)^T$. Its trace is $3+3=6$.
